passage: You asked how it felt, turning fourteen. Okay. I'm Pranav. That year I grew fast, and my arms got long and thin and my voice cracked. My cousin Leela, she's older, showed me photos of some boys online with huge muscles. I started comparing everything. I'd stand sideways in the mirror. I skipped dinner a few times, thinking it would make me look sharper. Then Leela noticed, and she felt terrible, I think. She sat with me and said those photos are edited, posed, lit perfectly. She said my body was still changing and would do its own thing. Our PE teacher said the same, and that if I was worried I could talk to the doctor. I stopped skipping meals. I still stand sideways sometimes. But I laugh at myself now.

qa.q: What did Pranav skip a few times?
qa.a: Pranav skipped dinner a few times.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when she noticed Pranav skipping meals?
qa.a: Pranav thinks she felt terrible, likely because the photos she had shown Pranav seemed to have started his comparing.

qa.q: What made the adults' and Leela's responses helpful?
qa.a: They explained that the photos were edited and posed, reminded Pranav that a growing body keeps changing, and pointed him to a doctor if worried, without shaming.

qa.q: What would change if Leela had never noticed?
qa.a: Pranav might have kept skipping meals and comparing himself to edited images, and the harmful habit could have grown quietly.

grounding: A teen describes comparing a changing body to idealised images, starting a harmful habit, and turning towards acceptance with support.

passage: I'm Mridul. Ojas and I have been in the same swimming class since Class 7. This year he started wearing a big T-shirt over his swimsuit, even in the water. Coach asked him to take it off, and Ojas went red and said he was cold. He wasn't. He'd been quiet in the changing room since some older boys joked about the hair on his chest. After that he missed two classes. I didn't really know what to say, so I told him that my shoulders are crooked and I've stopped caring. He laughed a little. Last week he came without the T-shirt. He still turned his back when the older boys walked by. Coach told them off for teasing and changed the lane groups.

qa.q: What did Ojas start wearing over his swimsuit?
qa.a: He started wearing a big T-shirt.

qa.q: Why did Ojas say he was cold when he wasn't?
qa.a: He was embarrassed about his body after the older boys' jokes and needed an excuse to keep covered without explaining.

qa.q: How did the coach help, and what else could Coach do?
qa.a: Coach stopped the teasing and changed lane groups; Coach could also have a private word with Ojas to check how he's feeling.

qa.q: What is it like for Mridul to watch this happen?
qa.a: Mridul seems unsure what to say and a bit worried, so shares a personal insecurity to make Ojas feel less alone.

grounding: A classmate observes a teen hiding his changing body after teasing, and gradually regaining some self-acceptance.

passage:
Week one: Urmila deleted her class photo from her profile because her face looked "round." Her friend Kashish commented, "You look nice!" Urmila didn't believe her. She spent the evening comparing herself with a filtered model's pictures.

Week three: In health class, the teacher showed how one photo can be changed with filters and lighting. Urmila felt oddly angry at how much time she'd wasted. She unfollowed several accounts that made her feel worse.

Week six: She and Kashish went cycling on Sunday and laughed so much she forgot about her face. At home she noticed she hadn't opened the mirror app in days. She reposted the class photo. It still felt strange, but she kept it up. 🙂

qa.q: What did the health teacher show the class in week three?
qa.a: The teacher showed how one photo can be changed with filters and lighting.

qa.q: Why did Urmila feel angry after the health class?
qa.a: She realised she had been comparing herself to images that weren't real, and felt upset about the time she had wasted feeling bad.

qa.q: What choices helped Urmila move towards self-acceptance?
qa.a: Unfollowing accounts that made her feel worse and spending time on active fun with Kashish shifted her focus away from her looks.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt when Urmila didn't believe her compliment?
qa.a: She might have felt sad or powerless, since her kind words couldn't reach her friend at that moment.

grounding: It shows a teen moving over several weeks from comparing herself to filtered images towards accepting her own appearance.

passage: Irfan, you've been skipping dinner and doing push-ups at midnight, I've seen. Sit, let me tell you something. At sixteen I had a poster of an action hero on my wall, all muscles. I looked at my thin arms in the mirror every morning and felt like a joke. So I started skipping meals and running in the heat, thinking I'd get that shape faster. At football practice one day, everything went white and I sat down hard on the ground. Coach Dsouza called my father, and we went to the doctor. The doctor said my body was still growing and needed fuel. Coach told me, 'That poster has lights and makeup and a team behind it.' I started eating properly and training slowly. Talk to me before you copy some poster, hah?

qa.q: What happened to the narrator at football practice?
qa.a: Everything went white and the narrator sat down hard on the ground.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel as a teen looking in the mirror?
qa.a: The narrator felt inadequate and embarrassed, like a joke, comparing their thin arms with the muscular hero on the poster.

qa.q: Why does the narrator ask Irfan to talk to them?
qa.a: The narrator has seen Irfan skipping dinner and training at midnight, and wants Irfan to get support before harming their health.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel hearing that the narrator went through the same thing?
qa.a: Irfan might feel less alone and more open to changing those habits without feeling judged. 🤍

grounding: An elder recalls teenage body comparison and harmful habits, and a healthier path with trusted adults.

passage: Swimming class started in twenty minutes, and the changing room was loud, steamy and crowded. Darshan, fifteen, stood in the corner with his T-shirt still on. He'd grown softer around the middle this year, and the boys in the reels he scrolled all looked carved from stone. He thought about pretending to have a cold. Madhav, already in his trunks, flicked water at him. 'You coming or what?' 'Maybe I'll sit this one out.' Madhav looked at him properly. 'Dude, half those guys online have filters. You beat me in freestyle last month.' Darshan remembered that race, the burn in his arms, the fun of it. He pulled off the T-shirt quickly before he could change his mind. In the water, he forgot about it.

qa.q: How long was it until swimming class started?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Darshan think about pretending to have a cold?
qa.a: He felt self-conscious about his body compared with the boys in the reels and wanted to avoid being seen.

qa.q: What helped Darshan choose to swim?
qa.a: Madhav reminded him that online images are filtered and that his body could win races, so he focused on what it can do.

qa.q: What might Madhav have noticed that made him look at Darshan properly?
qa.a: He probably noticed Darshan hesitating in his T-shirt and sensed something was wrong beyond laziness.

grounding: Shows a teen handling body comparison with idealised images and choosing a healthy activity.
